source_read: PDF, International Journal of Drug Policy 41 (2017) 74-79, all 6 pages read (pdftotext -layout). Pp. 75-78 (definition list, Fig. 1, Results, Fig. 2, Discussion) checked on renders at 150 dpi; Tables 1 (p. 77) and 2 (p. 78) at 300 dpi. The text layer drops some minus signs (e.g., CI -0.014 to 0.041 on p. 76), so intervals were read from the rendered page.

claims.overstatement: None as worded: the claim reports an association and does not say that missing autopsies caused deaths to be left out of the police count. Context worth keeping: the odds ratio is the adjusted odds of being counted only by the cause-of-death register (rather than by both) for deaths without autopsy, from a model that also adjusts for cause of death, drug and place, which themselves rest partly on autopsy findings. The police decide whether an autopsy is done, so autopsy status partly reflects police involvement. The direction of dependence cannot be read from these data.
claims.note: OR 2.66 (1.42-4.98), p = 0.002, n = 822 (715 autopsied, 107 not), confirmed on the rendered Table 2. Crude shares (editors' calculation from Table 1): autopsy in 284 of 367 deaths only in the cause-of-death count (77.4%) against 431 of 455 in both (94.7%); 715 of 822 overall (87.0%). The author asserts, without measuring it, that the cost and rules of autopsy mean some drug deaths go undetected and the figures may be too low (p. 78).

anchors.extracted: Persons in the cause-of-death register under the EMCDDA definition (n = 822), adjusted logistic regression of being only in that count versus in both registries: no autopsy (107) against autopsy (715), odds ratio 2.66 (95% CI 1.42-4.98), p = 0.002; the model also includes gender, age, cause of death, type of drug and place of death.

Autopsied: men in both registries 357 of 378 (94%) against 205 of 271 (76%) only in the cause-of-death count; women 74 of 77 (96%) against 79 of 96 (82%); men only in the police registry with a CDR match 38 of 47 (81%), women 18 of 27 (67%).

Physicians must notify the police of unnatural deaths, including use or suspected use of narcotics. The police decide whether an autopsy is performed, usually when the cause is uncertain and death sudden and unexpected, and are not obliged to order one when narcotics are suspected as the cause.

The author states that neither source gives the correct figure. Because of the cost and rules surrounding autopsy, some drug deaths will not be detected and the figures may be too low. A definition counting every substance detected at autopsy, whatever its role, would give a higher figure in Norway, where autopsy rates are high. None of this was measured.

claims.overstatement: None material. Omissions: (1) right after saying neither figure is correct, the author judges that the cause-of-death figures 'seem clearly' more complete and give a broader picture (p. 78), and argues both are probably too low; (2) the cause-of-death register held only Norwegian residents while the police registered all unnatural deaths regardless of residency, which explains part of the 33 unmatched; (3) stimulants also had higher odds than heroin of being in the cause-of-death count only (2.36, 1.16-4.76), which the list of drugs leaves out. 'First drug listed' is the first-contributing-cause T-code for persons in the register (Table 1, footnote b).
claims.note: All Norwegian numbers recomputed: 822 + 562 = 1,384 registrations; 33 + 74 + 455 + 367 = 929; 455/929 = 49.0%, 367/929 = 39.5%, 74/929 = 8.0%, 33/929 = 3.6%; dependence or suicide 121/367 = 33.0% against 35/455 = 7.7%; heroin 88/367 = 24.0% against 304/455 = 66.8%; women morphine/codeine 45/96 = 46.9% against 12/77 = 15.6%; mean age 42.7 (41.4-44.0) against 35.3 (34.3-36.2); 715 of 822 autopsied. Table 1 has two small errors that do not touch these figures (see the card check).

anchors.locator: Methods and materials, 3rd paragraph and the list that follows
anchors.extracted: The EMCDDA 'drug-induced death' definition as applied to the register: dependence codes F11-F12, F14-F16 or F19 as underlying cause; or accidental poisoning X41/X44/Y11 with T43.6 (psychostimulants), or X42/X44/Y12/Y14 with any T40.0-T40.9, as first contributing cause; or self-poisoning X61/X64 with T43.6, or X62/X64 with T40.0-T40.9, as first contributing cause.

Physicians must certify deaths and send certificates to the register (ICD-10 since 1996). The police registry rests on local police investigations reported to the national criminal investigation service; local and central police select deaths, including those with EMCDDA narcotics, and label them drug deaths. Drug information is free text, without ICD codes; autopsy results enter only if ready before submission. The register held only residents; the police registered all unnatural deaths. Linkage used the personal identity number, then manual matching.

1,384 registrations (822 in the cause-of-death register under the EMCDDA definition, 562 police) covered 929 people (11 matched by hand): 455 (49%) in both; 367 (40%) only in the register; 74 (8%) police deaths matched to a register cause outside the definition (23% with an unspecified cause linked to a disease); 33 (4%) police deaths unmatched, 39% of them not Norwegian citizens, the rest with missing or wrong ID numbers.

Compared with deaths in both registries, deaths only in the register were older (mean 42.7 against 35.3 years), more often coded as dependence or suicide (33% against 8%), less often had heroin as the drug (24% against 67%; among women morphine/codeine 47% against 16%), less often autopsied and more often in hospital or another institution. Adjusted ORs: morphine/codeine 6.89, methadone 3.69, synthetic opioids 4.63, stimulants 2.36 against heroin; no autopsy 2.66; hospital or institution 2.61; gender 1.05 (NS).

Neither the police figure nor the register's EMCDDA figure should be taken as Norway's correct number, and both may be too low (autopsy costs and rules; a definition limited to underlying and first contributing cause). The author nonetheless judges the register's figures more complete and broader; yearly trends in the two were similar up to 2009 (Fig. 1).

The author's proposed reasons, not tested: health personnel fail to report some deaths to the police and the police do not treat every drug-related death as suspicious (for the 367); a drug named on the certificate but not as the underlying cause, then adjusted by ICD-10 rules, and more complete autopsy information for the register (for the 74). Nordic autopsy series cited for a median of 4-5 drugs per case.

key_findings.correction: The definition pairs specific codes, which 'each combined with T43.6 or T40.0-T40.9' blurs. As printed: dependence F11-F12, F14-F16 or F19 as underlying cause alone; X41, X44 or Y11 with T43.6, or X42, X44, Y12 or Y14 with any of T40.0-T40.9, as first contributing cause (accidental); X61 or X64 with T43.6, or X62 or X64 with T40.0-T40.9 (suicide). So X41 never pairs with T40.x, nor X42 with T43.6. The design_detail field already has it right.

reporting_issues.note: Found independently: the column sums to 79; the women's overdose total of 128 and Table 2's 666 imply 66.
Found the 33-against-29 heading independently; the men's Total-column differences (354/353, 103/107, 19/20, 123/119) check out on the rendered table.

The printed differences can be reproduced from Table 1. The police group is the 529 police-registry persons with a CDR record (the 33 unmatched have no CDR variables), compared with the 822 CDR/EMCDDA deaths on CDR variables: male 425/529 against 649/822 = 0.014; at home 238/529 against 383/822 = 0.016 (police lower); under 40 341/529 against 442/822 = 0.107; heroin 310/529 against 392/822 = 0.109; autopsy 487/529 against 715/822 = 0.051; overdose 456/529 against 666/822 = 0.052 (0.054 printed; 0.053-0.056 with the misprinted 68). The card's 0.003 for autopsy came from counting the 33 unmatched as not autopsied. Still valid: the paper does not say the 33 were dropped or that CDR variables were used, and the two groups share 455 persons, so independent-sample intervals do not apply. The printed intervals are also narrower than a standard independent-samples interval would be (e.g., autopsy 0.018-0.083, editors' calculation, against 0.031-0.071 printed). The analysis.selective_reporting field and the notes for domains 7 and 8 should be amended to match.

risk_of_bias.note: Moderate fits. The domain 7 and 8 notes should drop 'not reproducible' for the first comparison (see reporting issue 3) but keep the overlap problem.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor. Point (3), that deaths certified as morphine may include heroin deaths, is an important caution for any claim about pharmaceutical opioid deaths.

missed: Table 1's autopsy count of 0 (0) for the 33 unmatched police deaths reflects missing register data (autopsy is taken from the CDR), not the absence of autopsy; the Methods list police autopsy results as a variable but Table 1 does not use them. Key finding 4 repeats the 0 without that caveat, and it is the source of the 0.003 recalculation in reporting issue 3.
